Q1.answer: Whether normalizing each input window of a forecaster with its own recent statistics (rolling-window normalization, RWN) removes the error caused by a post-deployment level shift, without harming accuracy when no shift occurs.

Q2.answer: Level shifts are described as the most common failure mode of deployed forecasters, and normalization with training statistics—which mis-scales every input after a shift—is used in essentially all forecasting systems.
Q2.missing: Supporting citations [R1]-[R6] are omitted, so the strength of these claims cannot be verified.

Q3.answer: In prior evaluations the authors examined, normalization and model size (capacity) were changed together, so the effect of normalization alone was confounded. No capacity-controlled test of per-window normalization under level shift existed.
Q3.missing: Only one source [R3] is cited for the confound; breadth of the gap is thinly supported.

Q4.answer: They generated SynthLoad (a synthetic hourly series following [R4]), added level shifts of s ∈ {0.2,0.4,0.6,0.8} training standard deviations, and compared three schemes on the same MLP over 5 seeds: baseline (training statistics), RWN (statistics of most recent 48 steps), and RWN-fixed (statistics frozen after the first 48 post-shift steps), measuring MAE.

Q5.answer: They fixed model capacity to isolate the effect of normalization (a capacity-controlled comparison), and added the RWN-fixed variant as an ablation to separate the benefit of re-computing statistics from the benefit of continued adaptation.
Q5.missing: The rationale for the specific 48-step window and the SynthLoad protocol choice is not justified.

Q6.answer: MAE was measured on SynthLoad with no shift and under shifts s = 0.2–0.8, for baseline, RWN, and RWN-fixed, using the same MLP across 5 random seeds.
Q6.missing: Per-shift numeric MAE values are not tabulated; only a no-shift pair and a percentage range are given.

Q7.answer: Without shift RWN and baseline were indistinguishable (0.409 ± 0.007 vs 0.412 ± 0.006). Under shift RWN reduced MAE by 11–29% for s = 0.2–0.6. Freezing statistics (RWN-fixed) recovered about two thirds of the gain.
Q7.missing: The 11–29% range is not broken down per shift level; MAE units/scale are unstated.

Q8.answer: On this synthetic series and at fixed capacity, RWN corrects moderate level-shift error (s ≤ 0.6) without harming unshifted accuracy, and most of the benefit comes from re-computing rather than continuously adapting statistics.

Q9.answer: It does not establish benefit at the largest shift (s = 0.8), generalization to real data, robustness across model capacities or tuned windows, or effectiveness for shift types other than level shift; nor does it truly separate capacity from stale statistics since capacity was never varied.
Q9.missing: The paper claims capacity is ruled out, but capacity is held fixed rather than varied.

Q10.answer: A capacity-controlled demonstration that per-window (rolling) normalization reduces error under moderate level shift without harming unshifted accuracy, together with a boundary at the largest shift and an ablation attributing about a third of the gain to continued adaptation.

Q11.answer: Synthetic data only, fixed model capacity, untuned normalization window, and only level shifts tested (no other distribution-shift types).

Q12.answer: Rolling-window normalization fixes moderate post-deployment level-shift error (11–29% for s ≤ 0.6) with no cost when there is no shift, but stops helping at the largest shift (0.8); most of the gain comes from simply recomputing statistics, not from continual adaptation.

location.quote: does per-window normalization reduce error under level shift without harming unshifted accuracy?

findings.observed: The problem is stated crisply and tied to a concrete failure (mis-scaling after level shift).
findings.reader_struggle: Adjacent readers may not grasp why training-statistic normalization mis-scales inputs after a shift.
findings.likely_consequence: B readers under-appreciate the mechanism behind the problem.
findings.revision_principle: Add one sentence explaining how a fixed training mean/std distorts a shifted window.

location.quote: Level shifts are the most common failure mode of deployed forecasters [R1].

findings.observed: A strong prevalence claim rests entirely on an omitted citation.
findings.reader_struggle: E cannot verify the 'most common' claim; A may dispute it.
findings.likely_consequence: Motivation reads as asserted rather than evidenced.
findings.revision_principle: Qualify the claim or provide a checkable source.

location.quote: RQ2: how much of the gain depends on continued adaptation?

findings.observed: Two explicit, well-scoped research questions are stated.
findings.reader_struggle: Minor: RQ2 assumes a gain exists before RQ1 is answered.
findings.revision_principle: Phrase RQ2 conditionally ('if a gain exists, ...').

location.quote: an ablation attributing about a third of the gain to continued adaptation

findings.observed: Contribution says 'about a third' while §3/Abstract say freezing 'recovers about two thirds', requiring the reader to reconcile the two framings.
findings.reader_struggle: Reader must infer that one-third + two-thirds are complementary.
findings.likely_consequence: Momentary confusion about the actual split.
findings.revision_principle: State both numbers together once and use one consistent framing.

location.quote: We generated SynthLoad, a synthetic hourly series, following the protocol of [R4]

findings.observed: The data-generating protocol is delegated to an omitted reference; no self-contained description.
findings.reader_struggle: B (told they cannot know the benchmark) and E cannot understand or reproduce the series.
findings.likely_consequence: Method is non-reproducible for the stated audience.
findings.revision_principle: Describe SynthLoad's generative process inline given the non-specialist audience.

location.quote: RWN reduced MAE by 11–29% across s = 0.2–0.6 (Figure 1)

findings.reader_struggle: E cannot check the trend or whether variance overlaps at each s.
findings.likely_consequence: Weak experimental transparency; claims hard to audit.

findings.observed: Only the no-shift condition has explicit numbers with dispersion; the units/scale of MAE are unstated.

objective_discrepancies: The objective promises the reader will know 'the benchmark used,' but SynthLoad's construction is delegated to an omitted reference [R4], leaving non-specialist readers unable to understand it.

The objective emphasizes showing 'how much of any gain depends on continuing to adapt,' which the paper answers, but the split is expressed inconsistently ('about a third' vs 'about two thirds') and without supporting numbers.
The objective asks the paper to show 'where the finding stops'; the s=0.8 boundary is stated, but the paper does not clarify the practical scope implication for the robustness audience.
